lead: A stick diagram is a topology sketch of a CMOS gate. It uses one line per layer — diffusion, polysilicon, metal — and a dot for each contact. It has no dimensions. It keeps only order and crossings. The sketch exists because a layout's electrical behaviour depends first on which pieces touch and which cross, not on exact widths. Designers use it to plan a standard cell, to check a transistor network against a drawn layout, and to find a clean gate ordering before drawing real shapes.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.6 for real widths and spacing, and Unit 3 for reading a CMOS gate as series and parallel networks.

blocks.text: A stick diagram is a map, not a mask. Each straight line is a whole layer. A diffusion line is the source-drain path. A poly line is a gate. A metal line is wiring. A dot is a contact between two layers. The top metal rail is VDD and the bottom metal rail is VSS: every pMOS source that must go high contacts VDD, every nMOS source that must go low contacts VSS.

A poly line crossing diffusion always forms a transistor; poly cannot cross diffusion as plain wiring. The poly is the gate and the diffusion below it is the channel. Metal crossing poly or diffusion with no contact dot is only a crossing, not a connection. If a poly column crosses diffusion where you wanted no transistor, you have drawn an unwanted device: route the poly around, break the diffusion, or change the column order.

items: Convention: diffusion green, poly red, metal blue, contact a black dot.
No dimensions in the sketch; widths and spacings come from Chapter 2.6.
Only order and crossings matter: which diffusion segment two transistors share, and which poly column comes first.

blocks.text: Shared source-drain regions show up in the sketch. Two series transistors can share one diffusion segment; that segment is a node, not a metal contact, unless the circuit needs it. Contacts drop from a rail to diffusion only at the correct source.

sections.h3: Euler path sets the column order

blocks.text: Write the gate as two networks. The nMOS pull-down conducts when the output must be 0; the pMOS pull-up conducts when the output must be 1. Series transistors are an AND condition, parallel transistors an OR condition. For y = ¬(a·b + c), the nMOS network has a and b in series and c in parallel with that pair. The pMOS network is the dual: c from y to an internal node n2, then a and b in parallel from n2 to VDD.

One continuous diffusion strip per side is best: it removes extra contacts and breaks. To draw one strip, walk through every transistor edge exactly once. That walk is an Euler path. The graph's vertices are the network's nodes; its edges are the transistors. The edge order in the path is the poly column order along the strip.

An Euler path exists only between the two vertices of odd degree. If every vertex has even degree, the Euler trail is a closed circuit: the strip returns to its starting node, so both ends of the strip contact the same rail or node. Use the same edge order on both sides; if that is impossible, add a diffusion break. Then place poly columns left to right in that order.

items: Draw the nMOS graph and the pMOS graph; mark VDD, VSS, y and internal nodes.
Find the odd-degree vertices on each side; the Euler path must run between them.
Walk the nMOS graph from one odd vertex to the other; if all degrees are even, start and end at the same vertex.
Do the same on the pMOS graph, keeping the same edge order if possible.
Place poly columns left to right in that order.

blocks.text: For y = ¬(a·b + c) the two sides share the order c, a, b. The n-graph (VSS, y, n1) has all degrees even, so its trail is a closed circuit: VSS–c–y–a–n1–b–VSS. Both ends of the n-strip contact the VSS rail, and the y segment carries the output contact. The p-graph has odd vertices y and n2, so its trail runs y–c–n2–a–VDD–b–n2: the VDD segment sits in the middle with a rail contact, and the two n2 ends are joined by a metal line.
The stick diagram fixes topology; Chapter 2.6 fixes dimensions. Transfer the column order first, then draw the diffusion strips, then the poly columns, then the contacts and rails.

items: Each layer line becomes a drawn shape of the width the design rules give, and each gap becomes a spacing from the design rules, all in λ.
Put contacts at VDD, VSS, y and any internal node that needs metal.
Check that every poly-diffusion crossing is a wanted transistor; count them.
Do not add a crossing to make the drawing neat.

blocks.text: For y = ¬(a·b + c) the finished static CMOS gate has 3 nMOS plus 3 pMOS transistors, so the mask layout must show 6 wanted poly-diffusion crossings. The stick diagram shows 3 poly columns because each input column crosses both diffusion strips. One missing crossing means one missing device; one extra crossing means a short or an unwanted channel.

figure.caption: The flow from a gate's schematic to a stick diagram. The Euler path sets the poly column order; each side then gets one diffusion strip.

spec.aria: Flow from schematic through the transistor networks and Euler path to one diffusion strip per side, three poly columns in order c, a, b, contacts and rails, and the finished stick diagram.

examples.question: For the CMOS gate y = ¬(a·b + c): (a) write the nMOS and pMOS networks, (b) find an Euler path on each side, (c) state how many diffusion strips and poly columns the stick diagram needs.
steps: Output is 0 when a·b + c = 1, so the nMOS pull-down must conduct when a = 1 and b = 1, or when c = 1.
nMOS network: a and b in series, c in parallel with that pair. Three nMOS transistors.
pMOS dual: output is 1 when (a = 0 or b = 0) and c = 0. Draw c from y to n2, and a and b in parallel from n2 to VDD. Three pMOS transistors.

n-graph vertices VSS, y, n1: edges c: VSS–y, a: y–n1, b: n1–VSS. Every degree is 2, so the trail is a closed circuit VSS–c–y–a–n1–b–VSS. Both strip ends contact VSS; the y segment takes the output contact.

p-graph vertices y, n2, VDD: edges c: y–n2, a: n2–VDD, b: n2–VDD. The odd vertices are y (degree 1) and n2 (degree 3), so the trail runs y–c–n2–a–VDD–b–n2. The middle VDD segment takes a rail contact; the two n2 ends are joined by metal.
Both sides use edge order c, a, b: three poly columns, one n-diffusion strip and one p-diffusion strip.
examples.answer: The stick diagram needs 1 n-diffusion strip, 1 p-diffusion strip and 3 poly columns, with column order c, a, b.
examples.check:
gates = ["a", "b", "c"]
poly_columns = len(gates)
n_strips = 1
p_strips = 1
print(n_strips)
print(p_strips)
print(poly_columns)

traps: A poly-diffusion crossing is always a transistor. Never route poly across diffusion as plain wiring.
Series and parallel swap between nMOS and pMOS. Write the dual; do not copy the nMOS network to the pMOS side.
An Euler trail runs between the two odd-degree vertices. When every degree is even the trail is closed, so both strip ends meet the same rail or node.
The same input order must be used on both sides; reversing one side breaks the shared poly columns.
Stick diagrams carry no dimensions, and a contact is not a transistor. Missing contacts leave a source floating; extra contacts short two nodes.

quiz.q: What does a poly line crossing a diffusion line mean in a stick diagram?
quiz.a: It means a transistor. The poly is the gate and the diffusion below it is the channel.

quiz.q: Why does a stick diagram carry no absolute dimensions?
quiz.a: It records topology only: layer order, crossings and shared nodes. Real widths and spacings come later from the design rules in Chapter 2.6.

quiz.q: For y = ¬(a·b + c), how many nMOS transistors, pMOS transistors and total poly-diffusion crossings does the static CMOS gate need?
quiz.a: 3 nMOS, 3 pMOS, so 6 wanted poly-diffusion crossings.

quiz.q: A stick diagram has a poly column crossing the n-diffusion but not the p-diffusion for input a. Is that necessarily wrong? Explain.
quiz.a: For a static CMOS gate, each input must control both an nMOS and a pMOS, so a column crossing only one side is a missing device. Check the network; only non-standard ratioed or pseudo-nMOS gates may differ.

quiz.q: Given pMOS graph edges c from y to n2, a from n2 to VDD, and b from n2 to VDD, give one Euler path and the poly column order.
quiz.a: The odd vertices are y and n2, so one path is y–c–n2–a–VDD–b–n2. The edge order is c, a, b, so the poly column order is c, a, b.

quiz.q: Where do VDD and VSS rails sit in the usual stick diagram?
quiz.a: VDD is the metal rail at the top and VSS is the metal rail at the bottom.

quiz.q: Why can a transistor network with no Euler path need more than one diffusion strip on a side?
quiz.a: Without an Euler path, one continuous strip cannot pass through every transistor edge once. The layout must break the diffusion and connect the pieces with metal, which adds contacts and area.

beyond: Not for the exam. Stick diagrams are mainly a planning and teaching tool; production layouts are drawn in editors and checked by DRC. The Euler-path idea still matters in standard-cell layout because a good column order reduces diffusion breaks and area. Modern finFET and gate-all-around cells use the same topology reasoning with fins and multiple metal layers. Search for standard-cell layout, Euler path in CMOS layout, and stick diagram to mask layout if you want to see the translation.
